title: Work
summary: In physics, work is the transfer of energy when a force moves an object: work = force × distance. Push the cart along the track in this model and the work counter climbs — and the cart's kinetic energy rises to match. No motion, no work: holding a bucket still does nothing, pushing it along B certain.

processes: Pushing the cart across the track
plainLanguageExplanation: Work in physics doesn't mean chores — it means energy transferred by a force moving something. The recipe: work = force × distance, measured in joules. Move a heavy cart far while pushing both matter: push 10 N and move it 3 m → 30 J of work. Two twists make work different from popular a: zero motion, zero work (holding a full suitcase nowhere does no work — you knee honestly tires, but the physics says nothing happened); and the more you push, the more energy you hand the cart. The work counter every meter climbed adds J. Push hard and far in this model and the cart glides faster, banks more kinetic energy, counter's crater states exactly how much energy your arms handed over.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: Energy transferred by a force moving an object

keyFacts.label: Formula
keyFacts.value: Work = force × distance (both along the motion line)

keyFacts.label: No motion, no work
keyFacts.value: Pushing a wall that won't move does zero work

keyFacts.label: Doubles either
keyFacts.value: Twice the force or twice the distance → twice the work

whyItMatters: Work is the currency of energy moves: every joule that transfers into a system does so as work. Physicists measure how engines, legs, and machines transfer energy in J of work. The rule 'no motion, no work' decides which pushes matter, how much energy athletes put into a ball, and how a ramp's force-doubling trades distance for effort — the same work done easier but longer.
tagline: Energy moved by force through distance
didYouKnow: Lifting a 1 kg mass 1 m vertically does about 10 J of work. Pushing a lawn mower through a 20 m lawn takes hundreds of joules — yet your muscles only turn about a quarter of the food energy into tile work; the rest leaves as heat.
